hook_text: In the Karoo there is a mirror the width of a classroom, and two hundred kilometres away, sixty-four giant ears listening to the sky.
clip_script: Your pupil is about seven millimetres wide. That is all the light-catching area your eye has. A telescope is a bigger bucket for light. Near Sutherland stands SALT, with a mirror about eleven metres wide, built from ninety-one six-sided pieces fitted together like honeycomb. It gathers millions of times more light than your eye. Above the atmosphere, Hubble's smaller mirror takes razor-sharp pictures, because there is no wobbling air to make stars twinkle. But light is only part of the story. In the Karoo, the sixty-four dishes of MeerKAT catch radio waves, invisible light that slips through dust and cloud, revealing cold gas, spinning dead stars and jets from black holes. Working together, the dishes act like one giant telescope. And they are becoming part of the SKA, the biggest radio telescope on Earth, with South Africa at its heart.
visual_style: A whiteboard eye with a tiny pupil, then a bucket labelled telescope, then SALT's honeycomb mirror, Hubble above wavy atmosphere lines, then rows of dishes in the Karoo joined by lines into one big circle.
pacing: A tiny eye, then bigger and bigger instruments, ending on South Africa's role.
